svg.title: A trust score means nothing until a risk score sets the threshold it has to clear
svg.desc: The trust score describes the subject right now and is built from static factors such as identity and role and dynamic factors such as location, time and patch state. The risk score describes the resource and rises with the impact of a wrong decision. As resource risk rises the trust score required to clear it rises too, so the same subject is allowed to reach a wiki and refused a payroll system. High trust plus high risk does not mean allow: it means allow with constraints such as step-up authentication, a time limit and session recording.
svg.text: Trust is about the subject; risk is about the resource
The score alone decides nothing — it has to clear a threshold that the resource sets
risk score of the resource — what a wrong decision costs
trust score of the subject — right now
above the line: cleared
allow, log normally, revisit on context change
below the line: refused
and the refusal must be attributable to a score
high risk, high trust
allow with constraints: step-up MFA,
time limit, session recording
a wiki, from a managed laptop
payroll, from an unmanaged device
same subject, different verdict
required
WHAT FEEDS THE TWO SCORES
trust score · about the subject
static: identity, role, department, device type
dynamic: location, time, patch state, behaviour
continuous — a login is a sample, not a fact
risk score · about the resource
what leaks, what breaks, what the regulator says
set by data classification, not by the request
it moves with the data, not with the user
the trap
A high trust score grants nothing
by itself. If the role is not entitled
to that resource, the answer is still
no — trust and authorisation are two tests.
so the decision is a pair:
is the subject trustworthy enough,
and is it entitled at all?
An access decision with no risk score has no threshold to clear, which is why zero trust projects that only add MFA end with stronger passwords, not a new architecture.
